span: Mere possibility of an alternative view on facts or interpretation of the contract does not entitle courts to reverse the
why: Headnote holding: a possible alternative interpretation of the contract is not a ground to interfere with an award.

span: A confession, which is made to a Police Officer, would be inadmissible having regard to s.25 of the Evidence Act
why: Headnote holding that s.25 renders a confession to a police officer inadmissible.

span: incriminating statements by the accused to the police suggesting the inference of the commission of the crime would amount to confession and, therefore, inadmissible under this provision
why: Court's own explanation that confessions to the police (and, by s.26, in police custody) are inadmissible.

span: Confession made to any member of the police, of whatever rank and at whatever time, is inadmissible in evidence in view of Section 25.
why: Passage narrates an earlier Supreme Court holding as a step in the court's survey; the present court's own adoption is not stated within the passage.

span: The confessional statement made by the accused before Military Police Officer alone is not admissible
why: Headnote holding: only a confession to a (military) police officer is barred by s.25; one to an army officer is not. For a confession to a police officer it opposes admissibility.

span: the confession recorded by the police officer is undoubtedly equated to a confession recorded by a Judicial Magistrate under Section 164 Cr.P.C.
why: Court treats a police-recorded confession as substantive evidence subject to safeguards; the passage does not name the special statute that permits this, so the condition match is uncertain.

span: Confessional statement made by the accused to a police officer while in custody not admissible in the evidence
why: Headnote: a confession to a police officer in custody is inadmissible, but s.27 admits the part distinctly leading to a discovery.
